memoryText: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
readingInstruction: Today there is no new reading. This week you opened the book of Hebrews and read three Psalms that Hebrews draws on. Take a few moments today to be still before the Son you have been reading about. If you have time, reread Hebrews 1:1-4 slowly.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Hebrews 1:3 is the center of the week. In a single sentence, it tells you who Jesus is and what he did.

“The radiance of the glory of God.” Light streams from the sun and shares its nature. You cannot have the sun without the light. In the same way, the Son is not a created messenger who tells us about God. He is God’s glory shining out. If you want to know what God is like, you look at Jesus.

“The exact imprint of his nature.” A seal presses a mark into wax, and the mark reproduces every detail. The Son is the exact expression of the Father’s being.

“He upholds the universe by the word of his power.” Everything that exists depends on him right now. The same Jesus who held a child and wept at a tomb is holding the galaxies together.

“After making purification for sins, he sat down.” This is the part most likely to change your week. He sat down. Priests in the old covenant stood daily, offering sacrifices that could never fully remove sin. Christ finished the work. There is nothing left for you to add to it. When you doubt that you are forgiven, remember that the one who made purification is seated, and the work is done.

Say the verse aloud. Carry it with you this week, especially into moments of anxiety. The Son who upholds the universe is the Son who has already dealt with your sin.
weekInReview:
This week you began Hebrews, the book that shows how the whole Old Testament points to Christ. You read the opening declaration that God has spoken finally in his Son, and you saw the Son’s superiority over angels. You heard the first warning against drifting, and you watched the Son become human to free us from the fear of death. You read the comparison of Jesus with Moses and the call to enter God’s rest while it is still called today. You saw that Jesus is a great high priest who can sympathize with our weakness, and you read the sober warning in chapter 6 alongside the anchor of God’s oath. In the Psalms, you sang Psalm 95, heard the voice of the Son in Psalm 40, and saw the priest-king of Psalm 110.

Behind it all stands a single truth: the Son is greater than everything that came before him, and he is for you.
reflectionQuestions: What does it mean to you that God has spoken finally and fully in his Son? Think about how you approach Scripture. Do you read the Old Testament as incomplete or as a story that moves toward Christ? What would change if you read every page as pointing to him?

How does Jesus’ priesthood change the way you approach God in prayer? Hebrews 4:14-16 says he understands your weakness, has passed through the heavens, and invites you to draw near. Think of a specific struggle or failure you have been reluctant to bring to God. What would it look like to bring it to him today, in the name of the priest who knows what it is like to be tempted?

Where are you most tempted to drift, harden your heart, or neglect your salvation? The warnings of Hebrews are meant to keep you close to Christ, not to frighten you away. Name one practice that could help you stay attentive this coming week, and one person who could encourage you in it.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the finished work of his Son.
Worship Jesus as the radiance of God’s glory.
Rest in all he has done.
